title: Google's data center took a village's farmland, no warning
description:
Google's largest AI data center outside the US took a village's farmland in Andhra Pradesh on clearances issued in nine days with no public hearing, a CESifo working paper reading US Census microdata found no statistically significant rise in unemployment among recent college graduates despite 94,046 tech layoffs through August, and the Department of Energy committed $1.9 billion to 31 grid projects to unlock about 23 gigawatts from existing power lines.

https://sharedsapience.com/the-century-report-september-27-2026/

This episode covers the Tarluvada land fight over Google and Adani's $15 billion data center, Australia's data center backlash, the Fairlie and Wu graduate-hiring paper versus the Stanford finding, the DOE SPARK grid-upgrade award, Microsoft's rebuilt Copilot and its persistent Autopilot agent, MIT's suicide-risk method for crisis text, and 16,000 exposed Supabase databases.

Get the written edition free, every day: https://sharedsapience.com/century-report/?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=description&utm_campaign=tcr-daily

In Tarluvada, Andhra Pradesh, a village lost farmland to a $15 billion data center built with Google and the Adani Group, approved on clearances issued in nine days with no public hearing, and three petitions now challenge it before India's National Green Tribunal. A CESifo working paper reading US Census microdata found no statistically significant rise in unemployment among recent college graduates, even as a tracker counted 94,046 tech layoffs through August with AI blamed in a third and little evidence it replaced anyone's work. The Department of Energy committed $1.9 billion to 31 projects across 26 states to fit sensors and stronger cables onto existing lines, unlocking about 23 gigawatts already stranded in wires run conservatively. Microsoft rebuilt Copilot around a preview-stage Autopilot agent it says could keep working after the user signs off, plus a planned Code layer Microsoft says will let eligible users build and host their own apps. An MIT team built a system that estimates suicide risk from crisis-line text, flags the exact words behind each assessment, and runs on an ordinary computer. And a security firm found roughly 16,000 Supabase databases exposing personal records to the open web.
